project.name: treetracker-android
project.description: Treetracker Android is Greenstand's native Android app for the Treetracker reforestation platform. Growers register tree captures (photos and GPS), manage grower accounts, and sync data to the Treetracker backend.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README to learn what Treetracker Android does: growers register tree captures with photos and GPS, then sync the data to Greenstand's backend. The engineering architecture guide then frames the whole codebase, describing the MVVM-with-Actions pattern, the Root/UI composable split, and Koin dependency injection that the rest of this tour walks through.

tour.title: Application Entry Point
tour.description: TreeTrackerApplication is the Android Application class that boots the process. It initializes Firebase, starts the Koin dependency-injection container, and sets up Timber logging before any screen appears. Everything else in the app is wired up from the DI graph it starts here.
tour.languageLesson: Kotlin/Android: the Application subclass runs once per process before any Activity. Registering it requires the android:name attribute in AndroidManifest.xml.

tour.title: Dependency Injection Graph
tour.description: AppModule is the heart of the app's wiring and the single highest fan-out file in the project. This Koin module declares providers for every repository, use case, manager, and ViewModel, so understanding it reveals how all layers connect. Because construction is centralized here, the classes in later steps stay decoupled and testable.
tour.languageLesson: Koin is a Kotlin DI framework. A 'module' is a lambda of provider definitions (single/factory/viewModel); dependencies are resolved lazily by type at runtime rather than by generated code.

tour.title: Navigation Host
tour.description: Host is the root navigation host that wires every screen destination into the Compose NavDisplay. Building on the DI graph from Step 3, it is where ViewModels meet their screens and where the app's flow between capture, signup, dashboard, and messaging is defined. It is the second-highest fan-out file, so it touches most feature packages.

tour.title: MVVM Foundation
tour.description: These three files establish the presentation-layer contract every screen follows. BaseViewModel provides observable state and event flows plus shared helpers for state updates, navigation, and action dispatch; Action is the marker interface every screen's action types implement; CustomTheme (the most depended-upon UI file) supplies the app-wide color, typography, and shape tokens. Together they define the vocabulary used by all feature ViewModels ahead.
tour.languageLesson: Jetpack Compose: UI is described by @Composable functions that recompose when observed state changes. ViewModels expose StateFlow, and the 'Actions' pattern routes user intents through a single dispatch function for predictable state transitions.

tour.title: Feature Screens and ViewModels
tour.description: Now apply the MVVM foundation to real features. The dashboard shows sync stats and routes into the app; the tree capture screen manages the camera, GPS gating, and feature flags; the signup ViewModel drives the multi-step account flow. Each pairs a Compose screen with a ViewModel that extends BaseViewModel from Step 5, showing how one screen is built end to end.

tour.title: Domain Use Cases
tour.description: Between the screens and the data layer sits the domain layer: small, single-purpose use cases that orchestrate business logic. SyncDataUseCase is the top-level orchestrator that uploads planters, sessions, trees, device config, and messages while reporting progress; the others build tree request payloads, upload individual images, and batch location tracks. Keeping this logic out of ViewModels keeps features thin and the workflows reusable by background workers.

tour.title: Data and Persistence
tour.description: This is where captures live on the device. AppDatabase declares the Room database and its migrations; TreeTrackerDAO is the central query surface (the highest fan-in production file) exposing CRUD and upload-status queries; TreeEntity maps a captured tree row with its imagery and upload bookkeeping; User models the grower. Preferences wraps SharedPreferences with typed, reactive accessors for session state.
tour.languageLesson: Room is Android's SQLite ORM. @Entity classes map to tables, a @Dao interface declares queries as annotated methods, and the @Database class ties entities and DAOs together with versioned migrations.

tour.title: API and Object Storage
tour.description: Captured data leaves the device as JSON bundles. ObjectStorageClient wraps the AWS S3 SDK to push images and data bundles to DigitalOcean Spaces. UploadBundle is the serializable envelope aggregating trees, sessions, tracks, and messages for one upload, while NewTreeRequest models a single captured tree. These DTOs are the contract the use cases from Step 7 build and the backend consumes.

tour.title: Background Sync
tour.description: Sync must survive the app closing, so it runs in the background. TreeSyncWorker is a WorkManager coroutine worker that invokes SyncDataUseCase from Step 7 and shows an ongoing notification built by SyncNotificationManager. TreeUploader does the heavy lifting: it uploads images, builds request bundles in windows, and marks rows uploaded in the DAO from Step 8, tying the whole capture-to-cloud pipeline together.
tour.languageLesson: WorkManager is Android's deferrable background-work API. A CoroutineWorker runs suspend work with guaranteed execution and retry, surviving process death, which is essential for reliable syncing on intermittent rural connections.

tour.title: Testing Infrastructure
tour.description: The test suite is large and leans on shared helpers. MainCoroutineRule (the single most depended-upon file across the codebase) swaps the Main dispatcher for a test dispatcher so coroutine-driven ViewModels can be tested deterministically. FakeFileGenerator produces reusable fixture data. The SessionUploaderTest shows the pattern in action, verifying an uploader against a fake database.
tour.languageLesson: Kotlin coroutine testing: injecting a TestDispatcher via a JUnit rule makes async code run synchronously and controllably, so tests avoid flaky timing dependencies.

tour.title: Build and CI/CD
tour.description: Finally, see how the app is built and shipped. The app build.gradle defines the Android application config and build types, while libs.versions.toml centralizes every dependency version in a Gradle version catalog. The GitHub Actions workflows build the APK and run the Gradle test suite on each change, and the play-store deploy workflow bumps the version and publishes a release, completing the path from source to store.
tour.languageLesson: Gradle version catalogs (libs.versions.toml) declare dependency versions in one TOML file referenced as libs.* across build scripts. GitHub Actions reusable workflows (workflow_call) let build and test jobs be defined once and invoked by multiple pipelines.
